title: Chapter 5: Object-Oriented Domain Modeling
description: Model a domain with behavior-rich classes instead of public data bags. Learners derive responsibilities from use cases, establish invariants in constructors and factories, choose visibility by ownership, replace hidden global state with explicit collaborators, and expose a small package API that can evolve without breaking its clients.

lessons.title: Packages, naming, cohesion, and public API design
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Packages, naming, cohesion, and public API design

## A package is more than a folder
The package declaration determines a type's namespace and package access boundary. Use lowercase domain-oriented names such as academy.ledger. A public type name should explain its role without relying on its containing folder.

```java
package academy.ledger;
public final class Ledger {
    public long totalCents() { return 0; }
}
```
Save this as src/academy/ledger/Ledger.java. A caller can import academy.ledger.Ledger or use its full name. Imports are compile-time name conveniences; they do not copy source, download dependencies, or change access modifiers.

## Cohesion and API size
Group types that implement one responsibility and tend to change together. Keep parsing helpers package-private when callers should interact only with Ledger. A public API should document units, null behavior, errors, mutability, and ownership. Once other code depends on it, changing those promises has a cost.

Naming packages only util, manager, or common often hides unrelated responsibilities. Organizing solely by technical layer can also scatter one feature; choose boundaries based on actual change patterns.

## Practice
Split the budget ledger into domain objects, console input, and a main composition root. Compile all sources with an explicit destination directory. Attempt to access a package-private parser from another package and explain the diagnostic. List the smallest public surface a second application needs. Draw dependencies and check that the domain does not import console or filesystem code.

exercises.title: Packages, naming, cohesion, and public API design: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What does an import declaration do?
hints: import is a compile-time convenience for writing a shorter name; it neither changes what a package-private member allows nor fetches any code.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 5 assessment

Use the chapter's explanations of invariants, validation order, and encapsulated mutation to solve the decision scenario and repair **Preserve state on invalid mutation**. Write a prediction of the resulting balance before running the debugger, and preserve the intended validation when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency: it checks one guarded deposit, not every constructor, visibility, or dependency-injection rule in the chapter. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for when the guard runs relative to the mutation, then explain that tradeoff without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 5 implementation lab: deposit
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `deposit`. Return balance + amount only when amount is positive; otherwise preserve the original balance. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Inputs have a nonnegative balance and any amount for which an accepted sum fits int. Nonpositive deposits leave balance unchanged.
hints: Translate "only when amount is positive" into a single guard that returns the unchanged balance for zero or negative amounts.
Trace the public 100+25 example plus a zero amount and a negative amount before submitting.

exercises.title: Preserve state on invalid mutation
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the supplied defect so the program writes exactly `10`. `withdraw` subtracts from `balance` before its `if (n > 10) return;` guard runs, so an oversized withdrawal has already changed the balance by the time it is rejected; preserve the demonstrated method call and explain why validating before mutating, rather than hard-coding the printed balance, keeps the account state intact.
hints: Reject a withdrawal larger than the balance before modifying state.

exercises.title: Ledger command processor
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement Ledger.run(String input). Process nonblank lines as exactly IN|amount or OUT|amount. Amount must be a positive decimal long; begin at balance zero. IN increases balance with overflow checking; OUT succeeds only up to the current balance. For each accepted line emit OK; for malformed, nonpositive, overflowing, or overdrawn commands emit ERROR and leave balance unchanged. End with BALANCE=<balance>. Join output lines with \n, without a trailing newline. Tokens are case-sensitive; trim surrounding whitespace on each line and token. Empty input produces BALANCE=0. Use long cents, not floating-point money. Do not hard-code sample outputs.
hints: Parse and validate all fields before mutating state. Split with a negative limit when empty fields must be preserved.
Choose collections according to identity and ordering requirements. Build output lines and join them with a newline.
